The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y,z)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t),y=y(s,t)$ and $z=z(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x,y$ and $z:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2xy,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}={x}^{2}-5z,\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=-5y.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2(st)({s}^{3})=2{s}^{4}t, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =(st)^{2}-5(s\operatorname{sin}⁡t)={s}^{2}{t}^{2}-5s\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =-5{s}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂s} & =t, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂s} & =3{s}^{2}, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂s} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂s} & =(2{s}^{4}t)\cdot t+({s}^{2}{t}^{2}-5s\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot 3{s}^{2}+(-5{s}^{3})\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡t \\  & =2{s}^{4}{t}^{2}+3{s}^{4}{t}^{2}-15{s}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t-5{s}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\  & =5{s}^{4}{t}^{2}-20{s}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y,z)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t),y=y(s,t)$ and $z=z(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x,y$ and $z:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x+z,\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=y+2z.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{s}{t}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & ={s}^{2}+{t}^{2}+s{t}^{2}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{s}{t}+2s{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂s} & =2s, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂s} & =\frac{1}{t}, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂s} & ={t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂s} & =(\frac{s}{t})\cdot 2s+({s}^{2}+{t}^{2}+s{t}^{2})\cdot \frac{1}{t}+(\frac{s}{t}+2s{t}^{2})\cdot {t}^{2} \\  & =\frac{2{s}^{2}}{t}+\frac{{s}^{2}}{t}+t+st+st+2s{t}^{4} \\  & =\frac{3{s}^{2}}{t}+t+2st+2s{t}^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, ${c}_{1}=1,$ ${c}_{2}=2$ and ${c}_{3}=2,$ and therefore

$$
{c}_{1}+{c}_{2}+{c}_{3}=1+2+2=5.
$$

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t)$ and $y=y(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-4\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2(2st)=4st, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂s} & =2t, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂s} & =2st.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂s} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s} \\  & =(4st)(2t)+(-4)(2st) \\  & =8s{t}^{2}-8st \\  & =8st(t-1).\end{aligned}
$$

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y=y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x+y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =x.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =2x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x+x\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y=y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{2xy}{{x}^{2}+1},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{2x({x}^{2}+1)}{{x}^{2}+1}=2x, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =2x+\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)\cdot 2x \\  & =2x(1+\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)).\end{aligned}
$$
